A Study of Life

The Naming
of Things

From sponge to sapiens, every living creature has a place on the great map. Here is how we drew it.

Classification  ·  Taxonomy  ·  Phylogeny
Begin
I Prologue

The Library of Life

Imagine a library where every book has been thrown into one enormous pile. Graphic novels, cookbooks, dictionaries, horror stories, math textbooks. Finding anything would be miserable.

Earth is packed with life. Some of it is obvious: dogs, trees, sharks, mushrooms, grasshoppers, snakes, whales. Some of it is easy to miss: bacteria on your skin, mold on old bread, microscopic plankton drifting through the ocean.

Some living things are familiar. Some look alien. Some move. Some stay attached to rocks. Some glow. Some sting. Some photosynthesize. Some hunt. Some absorb food like living sponges. Some are actual sponges.

So scientists needed a system. Not just a random "these animals are cute" system. Not "things that live in water." Scientists needed a way to organize life based on evidence. That system is called classification, and the science of naming and grouping living things is called taxonomy.

Classification helps scientists answer questions like: What kind of organism is this? What other organisms is it related to? What traits does it share with other living things? How did it evolve? Where does it fit in the story of life on Earth?

The deeper scientists look, the more classification becomes less like sorting toys into bins and more like reading a giant family tree.

If a dolphin and a tuna both live in the ocean and both have streamlined bodies, why do scientists classify dolphins as mammals instead of fish? What evidence might overrule appearance?

That last question matters. If you only look at where something lives, you can get fooled. Dolphins and tuna both swim. But dolphins breathe air, nurse their young with milk, are warm-blooded, and evolved from land-dwelling mammal ancestors. So classification is not just about looks. It is about evidence.

EvidenceWhat scientists ask
Body structureDoes it have bones, shells, legs, wings, segments, organs?
CellsDoes it have a nucleus? Is it one cell or many?
Food and energyDoes it eat, absorb nutrients, or make food from sunlight?
ReproductionHow does it reproduce?
DNAHow genetically similar is it to other organisms?
EvolutionWhat ancestors does it share with other organisms?
Why is appearance alone not enough to classify an organism?
Exactly. A dolphin and a tuna look alike because both evolved for ocean life, but they come from very different branches of the tree. Looks can be a clue. Ancestry is the answer.
II The Hierarchy

Eight Steps, From Everything to One

Classification works like zooming in on a map. First a planet. Then a continent. Then a country. Then a city. Then a single street.

Biological classification does the same thing in eight ranked levels. Each level gets more specific. A kingdom contains many phyla. A phylum contains many classes. And the species level is the most specific.

  • Domain Eukarya
  • Kingdom Animalia
  • Phylum Chordata
  • Class Mammalia
  • Order Primates
  • Family Hominidae
  • Genus Homo
  • Species Homo sapiens

That is a human, classified all the way down. We are eukaryotes. We are animals. We are chordates. We are mammals. We are primates. Classification is not just a label. It is a compact scientific description.

To remember the order, generations of biology students have used a single sentence:

Dear King Philip
Came Over For
Good Soup

That gives you: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Cheesy, but it works. Memorize the sentence and the order will stick.

Look at the pyramid above. What does it mean that humans and starfish are in the same kingdom but in different phyla?

III Naming Names

Why Homo sapiens Sounds Fancy

A jellyfish is not a fish. A starfish is not a fish. A koala bear is not a bear. A peanut is not a nut. Common names are a mess.

Common names change from place to place. The same organism might have different names in different languages, regions, even neighborhoods. So scientists use a two-part naming system called binomial nomenclature, which literally means "two-name naming system."

Each species gets a scientific name made of a genus and a species. The genus is capitalized. The species name is lowercase. Both are usually written in italics.

OrganismScientific Name
HumanHomo sapiens
LionPanthera leo
TigerPanthera tigris
Domestic catFelis catus
Gray wolfCanis lupus
Domestic dogCanis lupus familiaris

Notice that lions and tigers share a genus, Panthera. They are different species, but they are close enough relatives to live under the same first name. Notice also that dogs and gray wolves are barely different at all. Dogs are technically a subspecies of wolf.

This system matters because it gives scientists around the world a shared language. A researcher in Brazil, Japan, Kenya, Canada, and Georgia can all read Panthera leo and know exactly what is being discussed: lion.

Which is the correctly written scientific name for a human?
Correct. Genus capitalized, species lowercase, both italicized. Doing it any other way will get you a red mark in any biology class on Earth.
IV The Architect

Linnaeus and the Filing Cabinet

The man behind the system never saw a strand of DNA, never used an electron microscope, and lived before Darwin published a word. He still organized the living world.

In the 1700s, Carl Linnaeus set out to give every organism on Earth a place in a single ordered system. He grouped organisms based on visible traits, especially body structures. His system included ranked categories such as kingdom, class, order, genus, and species.

Linnaeus did not have the tools modern biologists rely on. He did not know about genes. He could not read DNA. He could only look, draw, dissect, and compare. And yet, with paper, ink, and stubborn attention, he built the structure that still organizes biology today.

Think of Linnaeus as building the filing cabinet. Later scientists added better files.

What kinds of mistakes might a scientist make if all they had to go on was what an organism looked like? Why might evolution and DNA change those answers?

V The Revolution

Darwin Changed the Question

Before Darwin, scientists grouped organisms by similarity. After Darwin, they began asking a deeper question: are these organisms similar because they are actually related?

In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. That book changed biology. Darwin argued that species are not fixed forever. Populations change over generations. New species can arise. Different organisms can share common ancestors. This idea is called evolution.

The Galapagos Islands sit about a thousand kilometers off the coast of Ecuador. Each island has slightly different conditions, and Darwin noticed that the same kinds of animals had different forms on different islands. His most famous example was the finches.

For example, bats and birds both have wings. But a bat wing and a bird wing are not the same kind of structure. Bats are mammals. Birds are birds. Their wings evolved separately. A bat wing is more closely related to a human arm than to a butterfly wing.

That sounds weird at first. Then look at the bones. A bat wing, whale flipper, dog leg, and human arm all have a similar basic bone pattern, because they come from a shared vertebrate ancestor. Two important terms come out of this:

TermMeaningExample
Homologous structuresSimilar because of shared ancestryHuman arm and bat wing
Analogous structuresSimilar function, different originBird wing and insect wing

A dolphin looks more like a fish than a wolf. But evolution says the dolphin is closer to the wolf. Looks can trick you. Ancestry goes deeper.

A bat wing and a bird wing are an example of...
Right. Bats are mammals and birds are birds. Their wings evolved separately for the same job. Function similar, ancestry different.
VI The Three Domains

The Largest Branches

At the broadest level, life on Earth splits three ways. Most everything you can see belongs to just one of them.

Most modern systems divide life into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. The divisions are based mostly on cell structure and molecular evidence.

Bacteria

Single cells without a nucleus. The unseen workforce of the planet.

Bacteria are prokaryotes, which means their cells do not have a nucleus. They are everywhere: soil, water, air, skin, intestines, deep-sea vents. Some bacteria cause disease. Many more are helpful or essential. They digest food in animal guts, ferment yogurt and cheese, break down dead matter, and cycle nitrogen through the soil. Bacteria are not "simple" in the sense of being unimportant. They are some of the most successful organisms on Earth.

Archaea

Also single-celled, also without a nucleus, but on a different branch.

Archaea were once mistaken for strange bacteria. Then molecular evidence revealed that they were different enough to deserve their own domain. Many archaea live in extreme places, like hot springs, very salty lakes, and oxygen-free mud. But others live in ordinary soil and water. They are a perfect example of how classification changes when better evidence arrives.

Eukarya

Cells with a nucleus. Everything you can see, and a lot you cannot.

The word eukaryote comes from roots meaning "true kernel," referring to the nucleus. If a cell has a nucleus, it belongs to Eukarya. This includes animals, plants, fungi, and protists. So a redwood, a mushroom, an amoeba, and you are all in the same domain.

You are more closely related to a mushroom than a mushroom is to a bacterium. Sit with that for a second.

VII Six Kingdoms

The Big Neighborhoods of Life

Many school systems teach six kingdoms. Whether you count five or six depends on the textbook, but the idea is the same: at a slightly narrower scale than domains, life sorts into a handful of huge groups.

KingdomDescriptionExamples
AnimaliaMulticellular, eat food, usually move at some life stageDogs, insects, fish, jellyfish
PlantaeMulticellular, usually make food using sunlightTrees, grasses, mosses
FungiAbsorb nutrients, do not photosynthesizeMushrooms, molds, yeasts
ProtistaMostly eukaryotes that do not fit neatly elsewhereAmoebas, algae, paramecia
BacteriaSingle-celled prokaryotesE. coli, cyanobacteria
ArchaeaSingle-celled prokaryotes distinct from bacteriaMethanogens, halophiles

Knowing the other kingdoms matters because it helps prevent common mistakes. A mushroom is not a plant. A seaweed-like alga may not be a plant. A bacterium is not an animal. A coral is an animal, even though it looks like a colorful underwater rock. Life is stranger than the categories we first learn.

For the rest of this lesson, we will focus mostly on Kingdom Animalia.

VIII What is an Animal?

More Than Just Furry Things

When people hear "animal," they think dogs, cats, bears, whales. But the animal kingdom is much bigger, and most of it does not have fur, bones, or anything you would call a face.

These are all animals: sponge, jellyfish, coral, earthworm, snail, octopus, spider, beetle, crab, sea star, shark, frog, snake, eagle, human. Some animals have brains. Some do not. Some animals have bones. Most do not. Some move quickly. Some barely move at all. Some look like plants. Some look like nightmares from the deep ocean.

Most animals share these features:

FeatureWhat it means
MulticellularMade of many cells
EukaryoticCells have nuclei
HeterotrophicMust get food by consuming other organisms
No cell wallsUnlike plants, animal cells lack rigid walls
Specialized cellsMany have tissues, organs, or organ systems
MovementMost move during at least one stage of life
Sexual reproduction commonMany reproduce using eggs and sperm

And the animal kingdom splits, most usefully, into two informal groups: vertebrates and invertebrates.

IX With and Without

Backbones, or No Backbones

When people picture animals, they usually picture vertebrates. But if you take the animal kingdom as a whole, vertebrates are only one slim branch.

A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone. Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Humans are vertebrates. So are snakes, frogs, sharks, robins, and whales. An invertebrate is an animal without a backbone. Insects, spiders, crabs, jellyfish, sponges, worms, snails, clams, octopuses, sea stars.

Most animal species are invertebrates. Insects alone are wildly diverse: beetles, butterflies, ants, bees, grasshoppers, mosquitoes, dragonflies, flies. And insects are just one group of arthropods. If animals had a group chat, invertebrates would absolutely dominate it.

X Body Plans

The Secret Blueprints

Animal phyla are sorted largely by body plan. And body plan starts with one elegant question: how does the body line up?

A body plan is the general structure of an animal's body. Scientists ask whether it has symmetry, a head, a backbone, segments, an exoskeleton, organs. They ask how it moves, how it eats. These traits help place an animal in a phylum.

Symmetry is the first big sorter. There are three patterns.

Asymmetry

Pattern
No clear arrangement
Example
Many sponges
Lifestyle
Attached, filter feeding

Radial

Pattern
Body arranged around a center point, like a wheel
Example
Jellyfish, sea anemones, adult sea stars
Lifestyle
Drifting, anchored, multi-direction feeders

Bilateral

Pattern
Mirror-image left and right sides
Example
Humans, dogs, fish, insects, worms
Lifestyle
Directional movement, head end, tail end

Bilateral symmetry is the body plan of an animal that moves forward. A head at the front is useful when sense organs and a mouth can be concentrated where the body is going. That sounds obvious, but it is a major evolutionary development. Most animals you can name have it.

A jellyfish is an example of which kind of symmetry?
Yes. Jellyfish are organized around a central axis, like a wheel or a flower. That works well for an animal that drifts and can sense food coming from any direction.
XI The Invertebrate Phyla

A Gallery of Strange Cousins

From animals with no organs to animals with three hearts and color-changing skin. Here are the major phyla in the invertebrate world.

Porifera  "pore-bearing"

Sponges. No heads, no brains, no organs. Still animals.

Sponges do not run. They do not chase prey. They do not have heads or brains or true organs. Adults usually stay attached to surfaces underwater. Water flows in through tiny pores, and they filter food particles from it. The phylum name Porifera means "pore-bearing." It is a very literal name. Sponges show an important point: an animal does not need a face, legs, or a brain to be an animal.

Cnidaria

Jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, hydras. Radial symmetry and stinging cells.

Cnidarians have specialized stinging cells that help them capture prey or defend themselves. They have a nerve net rather than a brain. A jellyfish is not a fish. It has no backbone, no fish-like fins, no fish body plan. The name is misleading. Corals are also animals, even though they may look like rocks or plants. Coral reefs are built by tiny coral animals living in colonies.

Platyhelminthes & Nematoda

Flatworms and roundworms. Two phyla, two body styles.

Flatworms have soft, flattened bodies. Planarians are free-living. Tapeworms and flukes are parasites. Flatworms have bilateral symmetry and a clearer front and back than animals like jellyfish. Roundworms are long, thin, and unsegmented. Soil nematodes, pinworms, and hookworms all belong here. Nematodes are everywhere. A handful of soil contains huge numbers of them. Being tiny does not mean being unimportant.

Annelida

Segmented worms. Bodies built from repeating sections.

Annelids include earthworms, leeches, and marine bristle worms. Earthworms are probably the most familiar. They break down dead material in the soil, mix in nutrients, and aerate the ground. Ecosystems do not run on glamour. They run on organisms doing jobs that matter. Earthworms are basically underground recyclers.

Mollusca

Snails, clams, octopuses, squid. Soft bodies, often shelled.

At first, a clam and an octopus do not seem like they belong together. One sits in a shell. The other has arms, intelligence, camouflage, and escape skills. But both are mollusks. Mollusks show that classification is not always based on first impressions. A snail and an octopus are relatives, even if one seems like a slow garden creature and the other seems like an underwater alien genius.

Arthropoda  "jointed foot"

The largest animal phylum. Insects, spiders, crabs, centipedes, and more.

Arthropods have bilateral symmetry, jointed legs, segmented bodies, and an exoskeleton. Their jointed legs help them move in complex ways. Their exoskeleton protects them, but it cannot grow with the body. So arthropods molt, shedding the old exoskeleton and forming a new one. That is useful, but risky. Right after molting, an arthropod can be soft and vulnerable until the new shell hardens.

Insects are arthropods, but not all arthropods are insects. A spider is not an insect. A crab is not an insect. A centipede is not an insect. They are all arthropods.

GroupExamplesKey features
InsectsBeetles, ants, butterflies6 legs, 3 body sections
ArachnidsSpiders, scorpions, ticks8 legs, no antennae
CrustaceansCrabs, lobsters, shrimpOften aquatic, hard exoskeleton
MillipedesMillipedesMany legs, two pairs per segment
CentipedesCentipedesMany legs, one pair per segment

Echinodermata  "spiny skin"

Sea stars, sea urchins, sand dollars, sea cucumbers. Ocean only.

Sea stars are often called starfish, but they are not fish. They do not have backbones, do not swim like fish, and do not share fish body systems. They are echinoderms, with a fascinating water vascular system that powers their tube feet. Tube feet help with movement, feeding, and gripping surfaces. Echinoderms are another reminder that ocean animals are not automatically fish.

Which animal is a mollusk?
Yes. Octopuses are mollusks, just like snails and clams. The shell got lost somewhere in the family tree, but the soft body and the muscular foot did not.
XII Chordata

All Vertebrates, And A Few Strange Cousins

Every animal with a backbone belongs to one phylum. That phylum, Chordata, also includes some odd relatives that lack backbones but share a deeper feature.

Chordates have certain traits at some point in their development, including a structure called a notochord and a dorsal nerve cord. For our purposes, the key idea is simple: all vertebrates are chordates. Now we can zoom in on the five major vertebrate classes.

Fish

Fish

Aquatic vertebrates with gills, fins, and (usually) scales.

Fish are ectothermic, meaning their body temperature depends mostly on the environment. They are extraordinarily diverse. A shark, a seahorse, a tuna, and a stingray are all fish, with wildly different bodies and lifestyles.

Amphibians

Amphibians

Frogs, toads, salamanders. Often start in water, finish on land.

Amphibians have moist, mostly scale-less skin, and most go through metamorphosis. A frog begins as a tadpole with gills and a tail, then develops legs, lungs, and an adult body. Amphibians are sensitive to environmental changes because their skin absorbs water and chemicals. They make excellent indicators of ecosystem health.

Reptiles

Reptiles

Snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodiles, alligators.

Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lungs, and most lay eggs with protective shells. Their scales reduce water loss, which helped reptiles thrive on land. One modern wrinkle: birds evolved from theropod dinosaurs, which means birds are deeply embedded in the reptile story. School charts usually keep them separate, but the evolutionary tree pulls them close.

Birds

Birds

Feathered vertebrates. Living dinosaurs.

The defining trait of birds is feathers. Not all birds fly. Penguins do not. Ostriches do not. Emus do not. But they are still birds. Birds are endothermic, meaning they regulate their body temperature internally. A chicken is more closely related to a T. rex than a crocodile is to a T. rex. That does not make chickens secretly terrifying. It does mean classification gets more interesting when evolution enters the picture.

Mammals

Mammals

Hair or fur. Milk. Endothermic.

Mammals have hair or fur at some life stage, and females produce milk for their young. Most give live birth, but not all. Platypuses and echidnas are mammals that lay eggs. Bats fly. Whales live in the ocean. Mammals are not defined by walking on four legs or living on land. They are defined by traits like milk, hair, warm-blooded bodies, and shared ancestry.

A platypus lays eggs. It has a duck-like bill. It has webbed feet. And it is a mammal. What evidence might convince a scientist that it really is one?

Humans are animals because we are multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic, and lack cell walls. We are mammals because we have hair, produce milk, and are warm-blooded. We are primates, along with monkeys, apes, lemurs, and tarsiers. Classification does not make humans "less special." It places humans honestly inside the history of life.

A monarch is an arthropod because it has jointed legs, a segmented body, and an exoskeleton. It is an insect because it has six legs, three body sections, and antennae. It belongs to order Lepidoptera, the group of butterflies and moths.

A sea star has spiny skin, tube feet, adult radial symmetry, and no backbone. Calling it a "starfish" is common, but "sea star" is more accurate. This is exactly why scientific classification matters. Common names lie.

XIV The Smallest Box

What Is a Species, Really?

A common definition: a species is a group of organisms that can reproduce with one another and produce fertile offspring. That works most of the time. Not always.

For example: a horse and a donkey can reproduce, and the offspring is a mule. But mules are usually sterile. They cannot have offspring of their own. So horses and donkeys are considered different species.

But species can be complicated. Some organisms reproduce asexually. Some are known only from fossils. Some species can hybridize. Some populations are caught in the middle of splitting into separate species. So scientists use more than one species concept, depending on what they are studying.

The basic idea is clear. The real world has weird edge cases. Science is often like that.

XV The Tree of Life

Drawing the Family Tree

The Linnaean ladder is still useful. But modern biology also uses something more visual: a tree.

A phylogenetic tree is a diagram that shows evolutionary relationships. It looks like branches splitting from common ancestors. The key idea: the closer two organisms are on the tree, the more recent their common ancestor.

A clade is a group that includes one ancestor and all of its descendants. Mammals form a clade. Birds form a clade. Some traditional categories get messy if they leave out descendants, which is why birds and reptiles can be confusing. Traditional school charts separate them. Evolutionary trees suggest that birds are part of the reptile story.

This is not a contradiction. The old categories are simplified maps. The trees are detailed satellite images. Both are useful, but they show different levels of resolution. Classification is allowed to evolve, too.

If new DNA evidence showed that two animals long thought to be distant cousins are actually close relatives, what should taxonomists do? Why?

XVI The Vocabulary

A Compact Glossary

Every term that earned its own definition in this study. Tap a word to revisit its meaning.

The vocabulary of taxonomy: classification, taxonomy, domain, kingdom, phylum, class, species, genus, binomial nomenclature, evolution, phylogeny, clade.

The vocabulary of body plans and biology: symmetry, vertebrate, invertebrate, exoskeleton, molting, ectothermic, endothermic, metamorphosis, prokaryote, eukaryote, heterotroph, notochord.

The animal phyla: Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Echinodermata, Chordata.
